questions.explain: 10 kWh is 10,000 watt-hours. Dividing by the fridge's 150-watt draw gives 10,000 ÷ 150 ≈ 66.7 hours - showing why a home battery is usually sized to cover only the most essential appliances during an extended outage, not the whole house.

questions.prompt: A household's solar panels only generate electricity while the sun is up, but the fridge, security lights and internet modem all need power through the night as well. What is the name of the device that stores the day's extra solar electricity as chemical energy so it can be released again after dark?
questions.explain: A battery bridges the mismatch between when solar energy is generated (daytime) and when it's needed (including night). It stores surplus daytime electrical energy as chemical energy, then converts it back to electrical energy on demand.

questions.prompt: A coal power station converts 100 units of fuel energy into 38 units of usable electricity, losing the rest as heat across several transformation steps. A solar panel converts 100 units of sunlight into 20 units of usable electricity in a single step. By how many percentage points higher is the coal station's overall efficiency, despite having more transformation steps?
questions.explain: 38% minus 20% is 18 percentage points. This shows that 'fewer steps generally means less waste' is a useful rule of thumb, not a guarantee - the coal station's efficiency at each of its steps happens to be high enough that, overall, it still converts a larger share of its input energy than a typical solar panel, even with more transformation steps involved.

questions.prompt: A house with rooftop solar panels but no battery loses mains power during a daytime storm, after a power line comes down nearby. Even though the panels are still generating electricity from daylight, a safety system automatically switches them off. What is the main safety reason for this?
choices: To stop the panels overheating in direct sunlight
To stop solar-generated electricity flowing backward into the grid, which could electrify lines that repair workers believe are switched off and safe
Because solar panels physically cannot generate electricity during a storm
To protect the (non-existent) battery from overcharging
questions.answer: To stop solar-generated electricity flowing backward into the grid, which could electrify lines that repair workers believe are switched off and safe
questions.explain: This safety feature exists specifically to protect people working on the grid. Without it, a solar system could keep a 'dead' line dangerously live from the house end, even while repair crews treat it as switched off - a serious risk after storm damage.

activity.title: Home energy audit: find the hidden wattage
activity.why: Shows they can use real specifications from the world around them, not the lesson, to reason about energy use - genuine data collection rather than description from memory.
materials: a torch or phone flashlight to read small print on labels
access to two rooms of the house with an adult
steps: With an adult, choose two rooms of the house (for example the kitchen and the lounge room).

In each room, find four electrical devices or appliances and look at their rating label or sticker (usually on the back, base or plug) for the wattage (W). If a label shows volts and amps instead of watts, note that separately.
Write down each device's name and its wattage - 8 devices in total.
Add up the total wattage for each room separately.
Note which single device across your whole list had the highest wattage, and what energy transformation it mainly performs (for example, electrical to heat, or electrical to light).
Count how many devices you found showing a standby light (a small light on even when the device seems 'off') across both rooms.
Record your totals and findings below.

record.label: Total wattage added up for room 1's four devices
Total wattage added up for room 2's four devices
How many standby lights did you count across both rooms?
Did most labels show watts (W) directly, or volts and amps you had to note separately?
Which single device had the highest wattage, and what energy transformation is it mainly doing? Explain in 2-3 sentences.

activity.check: Watch for a heating or cooling appliance (kettle, toaster, air conditioner, hair dryer) turning up as the highest-wattage device - heating elements typically use far more power than lights or electronics. If both room totals seem suspiciously identical, check the labels were actually read rather than guessed.

lessons.title: Reversible or irreversible: can you get the original back?
lessons.curriculum_text: compare reversible changes, including dissolving and changes of state, and irreversible changes, including cooking and rusting that produce new substances
lessons.intro: Melt an ice cube and you can freeze the water back into ice. Fry an egg and there is no way to un-fry it. The difference between those two changes is one of the most useful ideas in chemistry, and you can test it in your own kitchen.

sections.heading: The real test: can you get the original substance back by physical means?
sections.body: A reversible change doesn't create a new substance - it just changes the substance's state, shape or arrangement, and it can usually be undone by an ordinary physical process like heating, cooling, or evaporating. An irreversible change produces at least one genuinely new substance with different properties, and there's no simple physical way back to what you started with.

sections.heading: Changes of state: same substance, different arrangement
sections.body: Melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing are all changes of state. Ice, liquid water and water vapour are chemically the same substance - H2O - just with its particles arranged and moving differently. Freeze water into ice, then melt it back into liquid water, and you have exactly the same water you started with. That's a textbook reversible change.

sections.heading: Dissolving: reversible, even though it looks final
sections.body: Stir salt into warm water and it seems to vanish - but the salt hasn't turned into a new substance. It has broken into particles too small to see, spread evenly through the water. Leave that salty water somewhere warm until the water evaporates away, and the salt crystals reappear, unchanged. That's why dissolving counts as reversible: you can recover the original substance by a purely physical process (evaporation), without any new substance being created.

example.prompt: A spoonful of sugar is stirred into a glass of warm water until it disappears. Is this change reversible or irreversible, and how could you show it?
working: the sugar hasn't reacted to form a new substance - it has just dissolved into tiny particles spread through the water
evaporating the water (a physical process) would leave the sugar behind
recovering the original substance by a physical process is the definition of reversible
example.answer: Reversible - evaporating the water would leave the original sugar behind.

sections.heading: Cooking: heat that builds new substances
sections.body: Cooking an egg looks like a simple state change, but it isn't. Heat makes the egg's proteins unfold and link together in new, permanent ways - a chemical change. The clear, runny egg white becomes a white, solid substance with completely different properties, and there is no physical process that will turn a cooked egg white back into raw egg white. The same idea applies to baking banana bread: heat drives chemical reactions between the ingredients (including browning reactions in the crust) that produce new substances and new flavours, none of which can be undone by cooling the loaf back down.

sections.heading: Rusting: a slow chemical change with a very familiar product
sections.body: Rust forms when iron reacts with oxygen and water over time, producing a new substance - hydrated iron oxide - with completely different properties from the shiny iron it came from: it's flaky, reddish-brown, and structurally weak. That new substance won't turn back into solid iron no matter how you heat, cool or dry it, which is what makes rusting irreversible, in the same category as cooking rather than melting or dissolving.

key_points: A reversible change doesn't create a new substance, and the original can usually be recovered by a physical process like heating, cooling or evaporating.
An irreversible change produces at least one genuinely new substance with different properties, with no simple way back.
Melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing are changes of state - reversible, because the substance itself doesn't change.
Dissolving is reversible: evaporating the liquid recovers the original dissolved substance unchanged.
Cooking and rusting are irreversible chemical changes - heat, oxygen and water combine with the original substances to permanently produce new ones.
lessons.try_this: Dissolve two teaspoons of salt into a small cup of warm water, stirring until it disappears completely. Pour a thin layer into a shallow dish and leave it on a sunny windowsill for a few days, checking each day. Watch the salt crystals reappear as the water evaporates - proof that dissolving didn't destroy the salt, just spread it out. Compare this with what happens if you fry or hard-boil an egg with an adult: no amount of waiting brings the raw egg back.

questions.prompt: What is the key test for whether a change is reversible?
choices: Whether it happens quickly or slowly
Whether the original substance can be recovered by a physical process, with no new substance formed
Whether it involves heat
Whether it happens in a kitchen
questions.answer: Whether the original substance can be recovered by a physical process, with no new substance formed
questions.explain: Reversibility is about substances, not speed or location: if no new substance was formed and the original can be recovered by an ordinary physical process, the change is reversible.

questions.prompt: Melting an ice cube and then freezing the water back into ice is a reversible change.
questions.explain: Ice and liquid water are the same substance, H2O, just arranged differently. Melting and freezing don't create a new substance, so the change is reversible.

questions.prompt: Salt is stirred into water until it seems to disappear. What has actually happened to the salt?
choices: It has turned into a completely new substance
It has broken into tiny particles spread evenly through the water, but is still salt
It has been destroyed
It has evaporated into the air
questions.answer: It has broken into tiny particles spread evenly through the water, but is still salt
questions.explain: Dissolving spreads the salt's particles through the water - it doesn't change what the substance is. Evaporating the water would leave the same salt behind.

questions.prompt: Salty water is left on a warm windowsill for several days until only dry salt crystals remain in the dish. What process removed the water and left the salt behind?
questions.explain: Evaporation turns the liquid water into water vapour, leaving the dissolved salt behind as solid crystals - the physical process that makes dissolving reversible.

questions.prompt: Why is cooking an egg classified as an irreversible change rather than a change of state?
choices: Because it happens slowly
Because heat permanently rearranges the egg's proteins into a new substance that cannot be reversed
Because eggs are always classified as irreversible by definition, regardless of what happens
Because cooking doesn't involve heat
questions.answer: Because heat permanently rearranges the egg's proteins into a new substance that cannot be reversed
questions.explain: Heat causes the egg's proteins to unfold and link together in new, permanent structures - a genuine chemical change producing a new substance, unlike a simple change of state such as melting.

questions.prompt: Rusting produces a genuinely new substance (hydrated iron oxide) that cannot be turned back into the original iron by physical means.
questions.explain: Rust is a different substance from iron, formed by a chemical reaction with oxygen and water. Its different structure and properties mean it can't simply be reversed back into solid iron by heating, cooling or drying.

questions.prompt: Freezing water into ice and rusting a steel nail are both changes, but only one of them produces a genuinely new substance with different properties. Which one produces a new substance?
questions.explain: Freezing just rearranges the same substance, H2O, so it's reversible. Rusting reacts iron with oxygen and water to form a genuinely new substance, iron oxide, so it's irreversible.

questions.prompt: Banana bread batter goes into the oven runny and pale, and comes out firm, browned and smelling completely different - and cooling the loaf back down doesn't undo any of that. Was this change reversible or irreversible?
questions.explain: Baking drives real chemical reactions between ingredients, including browning reactions in the crust, building new substances with different structures and flavours. Cooling doesn't undo a chemical reaction, so the change is irreversible.

questions.prompt: Someone dissolves salt into water, then leaves the bowl in a closed, dark, airtight cupboard for a week. A week later, the water level and dissolved salt look completely unchanged, so they conclude 'dissolving must actually be irreversible for this salt, since nothing came back.' What process, needed to recover the salt, has effectively been blocked by sealing the bowl away from air and warmth?
questions.explain: Dissolving is only reversible if the water is allowed to evaporate, which needs airflow, warmth or light. A sealed, dark cupboard blocks evaporation almost completely, so of course nothing changed - that doesn't mean the process is irreversible, it means the right conditions for reversing it were never provided.

questions.prompt: Banana bread batter starts at 22 degrees Celsius and needs its centre to reach 180 degrees Celsius to finish baking. If the centre heats up at an average rate of 8 degrees Celsius per minute once it starts cooking through, roughly how many minutes would that take?
questions.explain: The temperature needs to rise 180 - 22 = 158 degrees. At 8 degrees per minute, that takes 158 ÷ 8 ≈ 19.75 minutes - close to a typical loaf's baking time, during which the chemical reactions that make baking irreversible are taking place.

questions.prompt: Rock candy is made by dissolving as much sugar as possible into hot water, then letting the solution cool slowly and undisturbed over several days, so sugar crystals grow on a string. Once large, hard crystals have formed, is this change reversible, irreversible, or does it depend on something else?
choices: Irreversible, because a genuinely new substance called 'rock candy' has been created
Reversible, because the crystals are still just sugar and could be dissolved back into water without any new substance being formed
It depends entirely on the colour of the crystals
Irreversible, because cooling can never be undone once it happens
questions.answer: Reversible, because the crystals are still just sugar and could be dissolved back into water without any new substance being formed
questions.explain: Growing crystals just rearranges sugar particles into a more ordered solid form - it's still sugar, chemically identical to what you started with. Dissolving the crystals back into water would recover the original sugar solution, which is exactly the test for a reversible change.

questions.prompt: A steel garden tool left outside during a Cooktown wet-season storm starts rusting within days, while an identical tool kept in a dry, air-conditioned shed shows almost no rust after months. Both tools are exposed to ordinary air with the same oxygen content the whole time. What is the one physical condition that differs between the two locations, and best explains the different rusting speed?
questions.explain: Since both tools get the same oxygen, oxygen can't explain the difference. The wet-season storm supplies far more moisture, and rust needs both oxygen and water together - isolating the one condition that actually varies is exactly how you find the real cause.

activity.title: Race the dissolve: does temperature change dissolving speed?
activity.why: Shows they can run a genuine fair test with repeated, timed trials, not just watch one reversible change happen once.
materials: warm tap water (not boiling - check with an adult)
steps: Prepare three cups with the same amount of water (about 150 mL each): one cold from the fridge, one room temperature, and one warm tap water that an adult confirms is warm, not hot or boiling.
Measure out 1 level teaspoon of salt or sugar to add for each trial.
For the cold cup, stir at a steady speed and start the timer the moment you drop the teaspoon in; stop the instant no solid grains are visible.
Rinse and refill the cup with fresh cold water, and repeat that timed trial 2 more times (3 trials total for cold).
Repeat the same process for room-temperature water, then for warm water, 3 trials each, always refilling with fresh water between trials.
Work out the average dissolving time for each temperature, and note your single fastest trial overall.
Compare the three average times.

record.label: Average dissolving time for cold water, across 3 trials, in seconds
Average dissolving time for warm water, across 3 trials, in seconds
Your single fastest trial time overall, in seconds
What did you dissolve?
Did warmer water dissolve the substance faster, slower, or about the same as cold water? Explain why you think that happened, and whether it changes whether dissolving is a reversible change.

activity.check: Warm water should dissolve the substance noticeably faster than cold on average, even though individual trials will vary a bit. Dissolving should still count as reversible regardless of speed - if the write-up says otherwise, that's worth a follow-up conversation.

lessons.title: Spotting a chemical change - and why the coast eats metal
lessons.curriculum_text: compare reversible changes, including dissolving and changes of state, and irreversible changes, including cooking and rusting that produce new substances
lessons.intro: You don't need a lab to tell a chemical change from a physical one - there are clues you can spot with your own eyes, nose and hands. And if you live near the coast in the tropics, you're living in one of the fastest places on Earth to watch a chemical change happen to metal.

sections.heading: Clues that a chemical change has happened
sections.body:
A few reliable signs point to a chemical change rather than a physical one: a colour change that isn't just fading, bubbles or gas being produced, a noticeable temperature change without anything being heated or cooled from outside, a new smell appearing, a solid forming out of two liquids, or the fact that the change simply can't be undone by physical means.

None of these signs alone is a perfect guarantee - ice melting changes state without any chemical reaction, for instance - but seeing several of them together, especially an irreversible result, is strong evidence a new substance has formed.

sections.heading: The chemistry of rust, briefly
sections.body: Rust is what forms when iron reacts with both oxygen and water at the same time - not oxygen alone, and not water alone. Perfectly dry iron in dry air barely rusts at all, and iron fully submerged with no oxygen present rusts far more slowly too. It's the combination that drives the reaction, producing hydrated iron oxide - the flaky reddish-brown rust you recognise - which is a genuinely new substance with much weaker structure than the metal it replaced.

sections.heading: Why the tropical coast is especially rough on metal
sections.body:
Cooktown and the surrounding coast combine three conditions that all accelerate rusting at once: constant high humidity (so there's almost always some moisture in the air), a long wet season (extending the time surfaces stay actually wet, not just humid), and salt carried in sea air, which settles on metal surfaces and speeds up the reaction significantly by helping current flow through the moisture film on the metal.

That's why boats, tinnies, roller doors, playground equipment, car underbodies, and cyclone shutters near the FNQ coast typically need far more anti-rust maintenance than the same items would in a dry inland town, even though the underlying chemistry - iron plus oxygen plus water - is exactly the same everywhere.

sections.heading: Protecting metal from that chemistry
sections.body: Every common rust-prevention method works by blocking one of the three ingredients (iron, oxygen or water) from meeting: paint and oil form a physical barrier that keeps water and oxygen off the iron surface; galvanising coats steel in a thin layer of zinc, which reacts with oxygen and moisture instead of the iron underneath, sacrificing itself to protect the steel; and stainless steel is an alloy that forms its own thin, stable, invisible oxide layer on its surface that stops oxygen and water reaching the metal beneath it.

sections.heading: A kitchen example of a fast chemical change
sections.body: Mix bicarbonate of soda with vinegar and you get immediate fizzing, a rush of bubbles, and the mixture cools slightly - three signs of chemical change in a few seconds, as the reaction produces carbon dioxide gas along with water and a dissolved salt. It's a useful, safe way to see the same category of change that rusting represents, just sped up from months to moments.

key_points: Signs of a chemical change include colour change, gas/bubbles, temperature change, new smell, a solid forming, or the change being irreversible.
Rust needs both oxygen and water together reacting with iron - remove either one and rusting slows drastically.
Rust (hydrated iron oxide) is a new substance, structurally weaker than the iron it forms from.
High humidity, a long wet season and salty sea air combine to make tropical coastal areas especially fast at rusting metal.
Rust prevention methods (paint, oil, galvanising, stainless steel) all work by blocking iron from meeting oxygen and water.
lessons.try_this: With an adult's permission, place one clean iron nail in a dry container, one in a container of plain water (fully submerged, no air gap), and one on a damp paper towel exposed to the air, ideally with a pinch of salt dissolved into its water. Check them every day for a week without disturbing them. Which nail rusts fastest? This tests the same three ingredients - iron, oxygen and water - that make the coastal climate here so hard on metal.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest evidence that a chemical change has occurred, rather than a physical one?
choices: The substance became slightly warmer or cooler
The change cannot be undone and has produced a substance with clearly different properties
The substance changed shape
The substance moved to a different container
questions.answer: The change cannot be undone and has produced a substance with clearly different properties
questions.explain: While gas, colour change and temperature change are useful clues, an irreversible change producing a substance with genuinely different properties is the strongest evidence a new substance has formed.

questions.prompt: Iron will rust just as fast in dry air as it does in humid, salty coastal air.
questions.explain: Rusting needs both oxygen and water to react with iron. Dry air lacks enough moisture to drive the reaction quickly, while humid, salty coastal air provides plenty of both, plus salt that speeds the reaction further.

questions.prompt: What two things does iron need to react with, at the same time, to form rust?
choices: Heat and light
Oxygen and water
Salt and sand
Carbon dioxide and heat
questions.answer: Oxygen and water
questions.explain: Rust forms from a reaction between iron, oxygen and water together. Iron kept either fully dry or with no oxygen present rusts far more slowly, because one of the two needed ingredients is missing.

questions.prompt: What is the general name for the flaky reddish-brown substance formed when iron reacts with oxygen and water?
questions.explain: Rust (hydrated iron oxide) is the new substance formed by this reaction - structurally much weaker than the original iron.

questions.prompt: Why does metal equipment near the Cooktown coast typically rust faster than similar equipment in a dry inland town?
choices: Coastal iron is a different, weaker type of metal
High humidity, a long wet season and salty sea air all combine to speed up the same rusting reaction
Rust cannot form in inland towns at all
Coastal air contains less oxygen than inland air
questions.answer: High humidity, a long wet season and salty sea air all combine to speed up the same rusting reaction
questions.explain: The chemistry of rust is identical everywhere, but coastal FNQ combines constant moisture, extended wet periods and salt in the air, all of which accelerate the same iron-oxygen-water reaction.

questions.prompt: Galvanising coats steel in a layer of zinc. How does this protect the steel from rusting?
choices: Zinc makes the steel completely waterproof forever
The zinc reacts with oxygen and moisture instead of the steel, protecting the steel underneath
Zinc removes all oxygen from the surrounding air
Zinc turns the steel into stainless steel
questions.answer: The zinc reacts with oxygen and moisture instead of the steel, protecting the steel underneath
questions.explain: Zinc corrodes in preference to the steel it coats - it reacts with oxygen and water first, sacrificing itself so the steel underneath is protected for as long as the zinc layer lasts.

questions.prompt: Vinegar and bicarbonate of soda are mixed and immediately fizz vigorously, releasing gas and cooling slightly. What kind of change is this?
choices: A physical change of state, like melting
Dissolving, similar to salt in water
A chemical change, evidenced by gas production and temperature change
No change has actually occurred
questions.answer: A chemical change, evidenced by gas production and temperature change
questions.explain: Gas production (bubbles) and a noticeable temperature change without external heating or cooling are classic signs of a chemical change - here, the reaction produces carbon dioxide gas.

questions.prompt: Painting an iron gate prevents rust mainly by making the iron a stronger metal underneath.
questions.explain: Paint doesn't change the iron itself - it works as a physical barrier, keeping oxygen and water away from the iron's surface so the rusting reaction can't get started.

questions.prompt: An unpainted steel gate bar loses about 0.4 millimetres of thickness to rust every year in Cooktown's coastal climate. The bar started at 6 millimetres thick and becomes dangerously weak once it drops below 3 millimetres. In about how many years would the bar reach that dangerous thickness?
questions.explain: The bar can lose 6 - 3 = 3 millimetres before becoming dangerous. Losing 0.4 millimetres a year, that takes 3 ÷ 0.4 = 7.5 years - the kind of calculation behind real maintenance schedules for coastal steel structures.

questions.prompt: A student paints one side of a single iron nail and leaves the other side bare, then leaves it in a humid spot for one week. The bare side rusts heavily; the painted side shows none. They conclude 'paint completely stops rust forever, on any surface.' Besides only running the test for one week, what is the other main weakness of this test, related to how many nails were used?
questions.explain: Testing with just one nail means there's no way to know if the result would hold up with different nails, paint thicknesses, or conditions. A trustworthy conclusion needs a bigger sample size, not just a single example, however clear that one example looks.

questions.prompt: Two identical unpainted steel brackets are installed at the same time: one on a boat used daily in Cooktown's coastal saltwater, one in a dry inland shed 200 kilometres away. After one year, the boat bracket is heavily rusted and the shed bracket shows almost none. Which explanation best fits the chemistry of rust covered in this lesson?
choices: The boat bracket must be made from a different, weaker metal
Both locations provide the same oxygen, but the boat bracket also gets constant moisture and salt, which speeds up the same reaction dramatically
Rust forms at exactly the same rate everywhere, regardless of moisture
The shed bracket didn't rust because shed air contains no oxygen at all
questions.answer: Both locations provide the same oxygen, but the boat bracket also gets constant moisture and salt, which speeds up the same reaction dramatically
questions.explain: Oxygen is available in both places, so it can't explain the difference. The boat's constant moisture and salt spray are the physical conditions that differ, and they're exactly what accelerates the iron-oxygen-water reaction on the coast.

questions.prompt: Galvanised steel has a zinc coating about 0.05 millimetres thick. In a coastal environment, that zinc corrodes away at roughly 0.004 millimetres per year before the steel underneath starts rusting. About how many years of protection would you expect from the coating before it's used up?
questions.explain: 0.05 ÷ 0.004 = 12.5 years. This is why galvanised coastal fittings - roofing, fencing, boat trailers - typically need re-coating or replacing after a decade or so, even though the underlying steel is otherwise still sound.

activity.title: Measure the fizz: how much bicarb makes the most gas?
activity.why: Shows they can quantify evidence of a chemical change (gas volume) with a real fair test, rather than just noticing that fizzing happens.
materials: string and a ruler, or a tape measure
steps: Measure 100 mL of vinegar into the bottle.
Using a funnel, add 1 level teaspoon of bicarb into a balloon without letting it fall in yet, then stretch the balloon's neck carefully over the bottle's mouth.
Lift the balloon so the bicarb drops into the vinegar, and let the reaction fizz until it stops completely.
Measure the balloon's circumference around its widest point using string wrapped around it, then measuring the string's length with a ruler or tape measure, in centimetres.
Empty and rinse the bottle, then repeat the whole process with 2 level teaspoons of bicarb, keeping the vinegar amount exactly the same.
Repeat once more with 3 level teaspoons of bicarb.
Record the balloon circumference for each amount of bicarb and compare.

record.label: Balloon circumference with 1 teaspoon of bicarb, in centimetres
Balloon circumference with 2 teaspoons of bicarb, in centimetres
Balloon circumference with 3 teaspoons of bicarb, in centimetres
Did you keep the vinegar amount exactly the same for all three trials?
options: Yes, exactly the same each time

record.label: What evidence in this experiment shows a chemical change happened, and how did the balloon size relate to the amount of bicarb used? Explain in 2-3 sentences.

activity.check: The balloon should get bigger as more bicarb is added, since more gas is produced, up until the vinegar itself runs out of capacity to react. Gas production and a temperature change in the bottle are the two chemical-change signs to look for.

lessons.title: Fair tests: variables, repeats and why one plant proves nothing
lessons.curriculum_text: with guidance, plan and conduct scientific investigations to answer identified questions or explore identified problems, including making predictions, and identifying variables and controlling them where appropriate
lessons.intro: A test can look scientific and still tell you nothing useful, if it isn't fair. Fair tests come down to a small set of habits - change one thing at a time, keep everything else the same, and don't trust a result from just one try.

sections.heading: Three kinds of variable
sections.body:
In a fair test, the independent variable is the one thing you deliberately change. The dependent variable is what you measure, to see if it was affected. The controlled variables are everything else you deliberately keep the same, so they can't be the real reason for any difference you see.

If you change more than one thing at once - say, both the amount of water and the amount of sunlight a plant gets - and it grows differently, you have no way to know which change actually caused the result. That's not a fair test, no matter how carefully you measured.

sections.heading: Why one trial isn't enough
sections.body: Living things and real-world conditions have natural variation - two seeds from the same packet won't grow at exactly the same rate, even under identical conditions. A single trial can be thrown off by something random: a slightly stronger seed, an unnoticed draft, a measuring mistake. Repeating a test several times and looking at the overall pattern, rather than trusting any one result, is what lets you tell a real effect apart from ordinary random variation.

sections.heading: Sample size: why testing 3 plants is riskier than testing 30
sections.body:
The same idea applies to how many individuals you test, not just how many times. If you test whether a fertiliser works using 3 plants, one unusually strong or weak plant can swing your whole result. Test 30 plants and one unusual plant barely shifts the overall pattern - the natural variation between individuals gets averaged out, and you can trust the result far more.

This is exactly why real studies of coral bleaching, for instance, survey many reef sites rather than checking a single patch of coral, and why sunscreen effectiveness trials test the product on many people rather than one.

example.prompt: A student tests whether shade cloth helps seedlings survive the wet season by growing 3 seedlings under shade cloth and 3 in the open, for one week only. Name two ways to make this a more trustworthy test.
working: 3 seedlings per group is a small sample, so one unusual seedling could swing the result
one week is a short time and only one trial, so a lucky or unlucky run of weather could distort it
example.answer: Use a larger sample size (more seedlings per group) and repeat the test over more time or run it again, rather than relying on one small, short trial.

sections.heading: Fair tests around FNQ topics
sections.body: Imagine testing which of three coatings best protects a steel nail from rusting in salty, humid coastal air - the kind of question that matters directly here. A fair test would use identical nails, identical salty-water spray, identical exposure conditions and identical measurement method (checking on the same day, using the same rust rating) for every coating, changing only the coating itself. Testing each coating on just one nail, or letting one sit in a sunnier spot than the others, would make any difference in rust impossible to trust.

sections.heading: Common ways a test stops being fair
sections.body: The most common mistakes are: changing two variables at once, using too small a sample, running only one trial, measuring inconsistently between groups, or letting an uncontrolled variable sneak in without noticing - like testing seedling growth in two different rooms that happen to get different amounts of light. Planning what you'll keep the same, before you start, is the best defence against all of these.

key_points: The independent variable is what you change; the dependent variable is what you measure; controlled variables are what you keep the same.
Changing more than one variable at once makes it impossible to know which change caused the result.
Repeating a trial several times helps separate a real effect from random, one-off variation.
A larger sample size (more individuals tested) makes a result more trustworthy, because natural variation between individuals gets averaged out.
Careful planning of what to control, before starting, is the best way to avoid an unfair test.
lessons.try_this: Design and run a fair test at home: which of two or three paper towel brands (or kitchen sponges) absorbs the most water? Decide your independent variable (the brand), your dependent variable (how you'll measure absorption - for example, how many teaspoons of water a fixed-size piece can soak up before dripping), and your controlled variables (piece size, water temperature, how you pour). Repeat each brand three times and compare the results, rather than trusting a single trial.

questions.prompt: In a fair test on plant growth, what is the independent variable?
choices: Whatever you measure at the end
The one thing you deliberately change
Everything you keep the same
The plant species used
questions.answer: The one thing you deliberately change
questions.explain: The independent variable is the single factor the experimenter deliberately changes, such as the amount of water given. What's measured is the dependent variable, and everything else kept constant is a controlled variable.

questions.prompt: A fair test can change two variables at once, as long as you measure carefully.
questions.explain: Changing more than one variable at once makes it impossible to know which change actually caused any difference you observe, no matter how carefully you measure. A fair test changes only one variable at a time.

questions.prompt: Why is it risky to trust a science result based on just one trial?
choices: Repeating an experiment is against the rules of science
Random, natural variation could make a single result misleading, unlike a repeated pattern
One trial always gives the exact opposite of the true result
Trials never need repeating if the equipment is expensive
questions.answer: Random, natural variation could make a single result misleading, unlike a repeated pattern
questions.explain: A single trial can be thrown off by one-off random factors. Repeating a test and looking at the overall pattern helps separate a genuine effect from ordinary chance variation.

questions.prompt: A study tests a new fertiliser on 40 tomato plants instead of just 2, so one unusually strong or weak plant won't swing the whole result. What term describes the number of individuals tested in a study like this?
questions.explain: Sample size is the number of individuals tested. A larger sample size generally gives a more trustworthy result, because it averages out natural variation between individuals.

questions.prompt: A student tests fertiliser effectiveness using only 3 plants per group. What is the main risk with this sample size?
choices: 3 plants always grow at identical rates, so the test is automatically fair
One unusually strong or weak plant could swing the whole result
Small sample sizes always overestimate an effect
There is no risk - sample size doesn't matter for plants
questions.answer: One unusually strong or weak plant could swing the whole result
questions.explain: With only 3 plants, a single unusual individual has a large effect on the average result. A bigger sample averages out that kind of natural individual variation, giving a more reliable result.

questions.prompt: Testing three rust-prevention coatings, a student sprays each nail with salt water a different number of times and checks them on different days, instead of keeping those the same for every coating. What is the general term for a factor like this that should have been controlled but wasn't?
questions.explain: Salt water exposure and checking time should have been controlled variables, identical for every coating. Letting an uncontrolled variable vary means any rust difference can't be confidently blamed on the coating alone.

questions.prompt: Real studies of coral bleaching typically survey many reef sites rather than relying on observations from a single small patch of coral.
questions.explain: This mirrors the sample size principle: surveying many sites averages out natural site-to-site variation, giving a far more trustworthy picture of overall reef condition than a single patch could.

questions.prompt: A test compares seedling growth under shade cloth versus in the open, but the shaded group also happens to get watered more often by whoever is caring for it. Besides shade, what has now become a second variable affecting the result?
questions.explain: For the test to isolate the effect of shade cloth, watering must be kept identical between groups. Letting it vary introduces a second, uncontrolled variable that muddies the result.

questions.prompt: In a fertiliser trial using only 3 plants per group, individual plants can naturally vary in height by as much as 6 centimetres just by chance, while the average difference researchers are trying to detect between fertilised and unfertilised groups is only 4 centimetres. As a multiple of the real effect being measured, how big is that random variation (random variation ÷ real effect)?
questions.explain: 6 ÷ 4 = 1.5. The random noise here is one and a half times bigger than the actual effect being measured, which means a small sample like this could easily show a 'result' that's really just chance variation between plants, not a genuine fertiliser effect.

questions.prompt: A single tomato plant given a new fertiliser grows 10 centimetres taller over a month than a single un-fertilised tomato plant. The gardener declares, 'this fertiliser definitely works.' What is the single biggest weakness in this claim, in a short phrase, related to how many plants were tested in each group?
questions.explain: With just one plant in each group, there's no way to tell a real fertiliser effect apart from ordinary chance variation between individual plants. A trustworthy test needs a reasonable sample size in each group, not a single pair of plants.

questions.prompt: A student tests whether rainwater or tap water helps seedlings grow better. They plant 10 seedlings, water 5 with tap water and 5 with rainwater, keep all 10 on the same windowsill, give them the same amount of water each day, and measure height after 3 weeks. Is this a well-designed fair test?
choices: No, because they should have used only one seedling per group
Yes - it has a reasonable sample size (5 per group), one clear independent variable (water type), and the other conditions are controlled
No, because rainwater can never be used in a real experiment
No, because 3 weeks is far too short a time to grow anything
questions.answer: Yes - it has a reasonable sample size (5 per group), one clear independent variable (water type), and the other conditions are controlled
questions.explain: This test changes only one variable (water type), keeps light, watering amount and timing the same for every seedling, and uses a sample size big enough (5 per group) to average out normal plant-to-plant variation - all the hallmarks of a well-designed fair test.

questions.prompt: A reef survey team knows that surveying just 2 sites gives very unreliable results, but accuracy improves a lot up to about 20 sites. If the team can survey 4 sites per day, how many days would they need to reach that 20-site benchmark?
questions.explain: 20 sites ÷ 4 sites per day = 5 days. Reaching a big enough sample size to trust the result, rather than stopping after just 1 or 2 sites, is exactly the sample-size principle covered in this lesson, applied to real reef monitoring.

activity.title: Fair-test two paper plane designs, and name your variables
activity.why: Shows they can design and run their own fair test with real repeat trials, and correctly identify their own independent, dependent and controlled variables - not just spot mistakes in someone else's test.
materials: a tape measure or a long piece of string plus a ruler
an open hallway or yard space
steps: Fold two different paper plane designs (for example a narrow dart and a wide-winged glider), using the same size and type of paper for both.
Decide on one person to do all the throwing, from a fixed launch line, so the thrower isn't a variable that changes between designs.
Throw plane 1 three times from the same spot with a similar throw each time, measuring the distance travelled to the nearest 0.1 metre each time.
Repeat the same process for plane 2 (three throws, same thrower, same launch line).
Work out the average distance for each plane design across its 3 throws, and the difference between your longest and shortest throw for plane 1.
Write down what your independent variable, dependent variable, and at least one controlled variable were in this test.

record.label: Average distance for plane design 1, across 3 throws, in metres
Average distance for plane design 2, across 3 throws, in metres
Difference between your longest and shortest throw for plane design 1, in metres
Which design flew further on average?
Name your independent variable, your dependent variable, and one variable you controlled in this test.

activity.check: The written variables should correctly name plane design as independent, distance as dependent, and something like thrower, launch spot or paper size as controlled. If the two designs' average distances are close, check the throws were genuinely similar each time - an inconsistent throw is itself an uncontrolled variable.

lessons.title: No lone genius: how science really moves forward
lessons.curriculum_text: examine why advances in science are often the result of collaboration or build on the work of others
lessons.intro: Textbooks sometimes make discoveries sound like one person's flash of brilliance. Almost none of them really work that way. Nearly every advance in science leans on evidence, tools and ideas that other people built first - and on teams of people checking each other's work.

sections.heading: "Standing on the shoulders of giants"
sections.body: The physicist Isaac Newton once wrote that if he had seen further than others, it was by standing on the shoulders of giants - meaning his own famous discoveries depended on centuries of earlier work by other scientists and mathematicians. That idea holds for almost all of science: a new discovery nearly always reuses evidence, equipment, methods or theories that other people spent years developing first. Nobody starts from zero.

sections.heading: Watching the reef: thousands of eyes, not one
sections.body: Tracking the health of the Great Barrier Reef - including detecting bleaching events - relies on combining information from many different sources: marine scientists doing detailed underwater surveys, satellites measuring sea surface temperature from space, and citizen science programs where trained volunteers and tourism operators record what they see on regular reef visits. No single person or team could survey a reef system that size alone; the picture only becomes reliable when many independent observations are pooled together and cross-checked.

sections.heading: Traditional knowledge and modern science, working together
sections.body: Indigenous ranger programs, run by Traditional Owner groups across northern Australia, increasingly combine land and sea management knowledge - built up and passed down over an extremely long time - with modern scientific tools like satellite tracking, water testing and population surveys. Neither source of knowledge replaces the other; specific, long-term local knowledge of Country and rigorous modern measurement tools genuinely strengthen each other when the people holding them work together.

sections.heading: Big problems need big collaborations
sections.body: Some scientific challenges are simply too large for any single lab or country. Tracking a cyclone's path and intensity as it approaches the Queensland coast draws on satellite data, weather models and observations shared between meteorological agencies in multiple countries, feeding into the forecasts your family checks before a storm. Vaccine development is another example - large, complex problems typically get solved faster, and more reliably, when many researchers around the world share data and results rather than working in isolation.

sections.heading: Why scientists check each other's work
sections.body: Before most scientific results are accepted, other scientists who weren't involved in the original study review the methods and evidence - a process called peer review - and other labs often try to reproduce the result independently. This isn't scientists doubting each other for no reason: it's a system built to catch mistakes, spot problems with a method, and confirm a result is solid before it becomes something other scientists build further work on. Science advances fastest when results are shared openly enough for this checking to happen.

key_points: Scientific discoveries almost always build on evidence, tools and theories developed by earlier researchers, not from a single flash of insight.
Reef monitoring combines underwater surveys, satellite data and citizen science, because no one source can cover a system that large alone.
Traditional Owner ranger programs increasingly combine long-held knowledge of Country with modern scientific tools, strengthening both.
Large problems - like cyclone forecasting or vaccine development - are typically solved faster through international collaboration and shared data.
Peer review and independent replication let other scientists check a result before it's trusted and built upon.
lessons.try_this: Run a two-person data check, like scientists do with peer review. Pick something easy to count for two minutes - ants near a snack, cars passing the house, birds in a tree - and have two people count it separately, without comparing notes while counting. Then compare your two tallies. Are they the same? If not, discuss why (missed one, miscounted, defined "counts" differently) - this is exactly the kind of checking that happens when a second scientist reviews someone else's results.

questions.prompt: Most major scientific discoveries happen because one person works entirely alone, without relying on any previous research.
questions.explain: Almost all scientific advances build on evidence, tools and theories developed by earlier researchers. Even famous individual discoveries typically depend on a large body of earlier collaborative work.

questions.prompt: What did Isaac Newton mean by saying he saw further by "standing on the shoulders of giants"?
choices: That he was taller than most other scientists
That his discoveries depended on centuries of earlier work by other scientists and mathematicians
That science is best done by working completely alone
That he literally stood on other people's shoulders to see
questions.answer: That his discoveries depended on centuries of earlier work by other scientists and mathematicians
questions.explain: It's a metaphor: Newton was acknowledging that his own famous discoveries were only possible because of the huge amount of earlier work by other researchers that he was able to build on.

questions.prompt: Why does tracking the health of the Great Barrier Reef rely on combining underwater surveys, satellite data and citizen science, rather than just one of these?
choices: Because satellites alone give a perfectly complete picture
Because the reef system is too large for any single source to monitor alone, and combining independent sources gives a more reliable picture
Because citizen science is more accurate than professional surveys
Because underwater surveys are no longer allowed
questions.answer: Because the reef system is too large for any single source to monitor alone, and combining independent sources gives a more reliable picture
questions.explain: The Great Barrier Reef is far too large for any one method to cover completely. Combining and cross-checking multiple independent sources gives a much more complete and trustworthy picture.

questions.prompt: Before a surprising new result is widely accepted, other scientists who weren't involved in the study check its methods and evidence. What is this checking process called?
questions.explain: Peer review is this checking process, designed to catch mistakes and confirm a result is solid before other scientists start building further work on top of it.

questions.prompt: How do Indigenous ranger programs across northern Australia often combine traditional knowledge with modern science?
choices: They replace traditional knowledge entirely with satellite data
They combine long-held knowledge of Country with modern tools like satellite tracking and water testing, strengthening both
They keep traditional knowledge and modern science completely separate
They only use methods that existed before modern technology
questions.answer: They combine long-held knowledge of Country with modern tools like satellite tracking and water testing, strengthening both
questions.explain: These programs typically bring long-term, detailed knowledge of Country together with modern scientific tools - neither replaces the other, and combining them gives a stronger result than either alone.

questions.prompt: International collaboration, such as sharing satellite data and weather models between countries, plays a major role in forecasting a cyclone's path toward the Queensland coast.
questions.explain: Cyclone forecasting draws on data and models shared between meteorological agencies in multiple countries. No single country's data alone would produce as reliable a forecast.

questions.prompt: A researcher publishes surprising results but refuses to share their data or methods with other scientists. Why would this concern the scientific community?
choices: It would not concern anyone, since results only need to be announced
It prevents peer review and independent replication, which are how results normally get checked before being trusted
Sharing data is only required for very small studies
Scientists are legally required to keep their data private
questions.answer: It prevents peer review and independent replication, which are how results normally get checked before being trusted
questions.explain: Without shared data and methods, other scientists can't properly review or attempt to reproduce the result. That checking process is central to how science builds reliable, trusted knowledge.

questions.prompt: Which of these best explains why large problems, like developing a new vaccine, are usually tackled by big international collaborations rather than a single lab?
choices: Because a single lab is not allowed to do this kind of research
Because such problems require huge amounts of data, testing and expertise that no single lab could gather alone, so pooling effort speeds up reliable progress
Because collaboration is required by law for all scientific research
Because a single lab would solve it just as fast, but collaboration is done out of tradition
questions.answer: Because such problems require huge amounts of data, testing and expertise that no single lab could gather alone, so pooling effort speeds up reliable progress
questions.explain: Problems of this scale need more data, more testing capacity and more specialised expertise than any one lab has. Sharing the work across many researchers and institutions gets to a reliable answer faster.

questions.prompt: A single small lab tests a new vaccine on 40 volunteers and estimates it's 70% effective. A large international collaboration pools data from 12 countries and tests 40,000 volunteers, estimating 65% effective. Roughly how many times bigger is the international collaboration's sample size than the single lab's?
questions.explain: 40,000 ÷ 40 = 1,000. A sample a thousand times bigger, pooled across many countries, gives a far more trustworthy estimate than one small lab's result, even though the two percentages look fairly close - this is exactly why large collaborations are trusted more than isolated small studies.

questions.prompt: A research group claims to have found a new marker of coral resilience to heat stress but declines to share their raw data or exact methods with other scientists, so other labs can't check it. What is the name of the specific process being blocked here - independent labs trying to get the same result themselves, using their own attempt at the same method?
questions.explain: Replication is when other, independent researchers repeat a study to see if they get the same result. Without shared data and methods, replication becomes impossible, which is exactly why refusing to share raises concern in the scientific community.

questions.prompt: Traditional Owner rangers notice mangrove dieback in one area and want to know if it's linked to a marine heatwave. They combine their long-term on-Country observations with satellite sea-surface-temperature data and a marine scientist's water testing. Why does combining these three sources give a stronger conclusion than any one of them alone?
choices: Because satellite data is always more accurate than any other kind of evidence
Each source can confirm or challenge the others, and together they cover things - long-term local change, broad temperature patterns, precise water chemistry - that no single method captures alone
Because using exactly three methods is a legal requirement for environmental research
Because rangers' direct observations should be set aside in favour of satellite data
questions.answer: Each source can confirm or challenge the others, and together they cover things - long-term local change, broad temperature patterns, precise water chemistry - that no single method captures alone
questions.explain: Combining independent sources lets each one check the others and fill in gaps the others miss. Long-term local knowledge, wide-area satellite data and precise on-site testing each capture something the others can't, which is why using all three together is more convincing than relying on just one.

questions.prompt: A cyclone forecast using only one country's satellite data has historically been accurate to within about 150 kilometres of the actual landfall location, 3 days ahead. When several countries' data and models are combined, that same 3-day forecast improves to within about 60 kilometres. By how many kilometres does combining data reduce the average forecast error?
questions.explain: 150 - 60 = 90 kilometres of improvement. Pooling satellite data and models from multiple countries genuinely sharpens cyclone forecasts, which is exactly the kind of international collaboration that gets built into the warnings families along the Queensland coast rely on.

activity.title: Run your own three-trial replication study
activity.why: Shows they can quantify how reliable independent observations really are when repeated - the actual practice of scientific replication, not just a one-off demonstration of checking.
materials: something countable outside (cars passing, birds in a tree, ants at a food scrap, moths at a light)
steps: Choose something you and a partner can both observe and count for exactly 2 minutes.
Set a timer for 2 minutes. Both people count independently, without saying numbers out loud or looking at each other's tally, until the timer stops.
Compare your two counts, record both, and work out the percentage difference between them: (difference ÷ average of the two counts) × 100.
Repeat this for two more separate 2-minute trials, either counting the same thing at a different time or a different thing each time, always counting independently.
Work out the percentage difference for each of the three trials.

Discuss with your co-counter why any differences happened (missed one, double-counted, disagreed on what counts) - this is exactly the kind of discussion that happens in real peer review and replication.

record.label: Percentage difference between the two counts in trial 1
Percentage difference between the two counts in trial 2
Percentage difference between the two counts in trial 3
What did you count across your three trials?
What caused the biggest disagreement between counters, and what would you change to make your counting method more reliable next time?

activity.check: Some disagreement between counters is normal and expected - a percentage difference of zero every single trial is actually a little suspicious. The written discussion should name a real, specific reason for any mismatch (missed count, different starting moment, disagreement on what counted), not just restate that they disagreed.
